planting.note: Direct sow once soil is thoroughly warm; broomcorn needs a long, hot summer to fully develop its brush before frost.

directions: Broomcorn is a specialty sorghum grown not for its small, mostly inedible seed but for its 'brush' — the long, wiry, fibrous seed-head branches that were the traditional raw material for handmade brooms. It is field-grown like grain sorghum but harvested differently: stalks are cut or bent over ('tabled') just as the brush straightens and seed begins to color, since waiting too long lets the fiber lose its flexibility and turn brittle. After cutting, the brush is stripped from the stalk, tied into small hands, and hung or laid out to cure and dry for one to two weeks before the individual straws are cleaned of seed and sorted by length for weaving into hand brooms or whisks. Distinguishing traits from grain, syrup, and forage sorghum types already grown for cereal, sweet cane, or livestock feed: broomcorn's seed head is a loose, elongated panicle of long straight fibers rather than a dense compact grain head, bred over centuries specifically for that structural fiber quality.

planting.note: Direct sow after danger of frost has passed; this heirloom needs a full warm season to size up its dye-producing seed heads.

directions: This is a Hopi heirloom grown specifically for its hull color rather than for eating or oil pressing: the seed coats are an intensely deep purple-black that, when the whole seeds are simmered in water, release a rich purple-to-black dye historically used by Hopi dyers for coloring wool, basketry fiber, and leather. Grow it exactly as any tall single-stem sunflower, in fertile soil with full sun, and allow the large flower heads to fully mature and dry on the stalk until the backs turn brown and seeds are firm. Because the dye compound is concentrated in the hull rather than the kernel, gardeners harvest whole dried seed heads, thresh out the seed, and simmer the unshelled seed directly to make dyebath rather than dehulling first as one would for a culinary or oilseed sunflower. Distinguishing it from every other sunflower cultivar in cultivation is this specific, reliably dark seed-coat pigment, selected and maintained by Hopi growers over many generations for craft and textile use rather than for food.

planting.note: Direct-sow in late summer or fall for a first-year basal rosette that bolts and flowers in its second year, biennial-fashion; a spring sowing works too but delays flowering to the following year.

directions: Fuller's teasel is grown not for fiber or pigment itself but as the traditional tool used to process fiber: its dense, egg-shaped seed heads are ringed with stiff, backward-hooking spines that were historically mounted on frames or wheels ('teasel gigs') and dragged across woven woolen cloth to raise a soft nap before shearing it smooth, a step still done by hand by small-scale fiber artisans and hand-weavers today. It grows as a coarse biennial rosette the first year, then sends up a tall, spiny-stemmed flower stalk topped with cone-like flower heads in its second summer; cut the mature seed heads once they have dried to a stiff tan-brown color and their small purple flowers have fully finished, then hang them to finish curing before use. This cultivated form is selected for firmer, straighter, more strongly recurved bracts than its weedy relative, common or wild teasel (Dipsacus fullonum), whose softer, straighter spines make it far less useful for napping cloth. Because the species can self-sow aggressively, cut and remove spent seed heads promptly if naturalizing beyond a contained bed is a concern.

planting.note: Start seed indoors after a period of cold stratification, since germination is slow and irregular; set out transplants after last frost into a permanent bed, as the dye-bearing taproot needs two to three years to size up before harvest.

directions: Purple gromwell, known in Japan as murasaki, is grown for its thick, woody taproot, whose outer bark layer contains shikonin, a naphthoquinone pigment that yields a distinctive deep reddish-purple dye once used for imperial court robes and prized kimono silk. The plant itself is an unassuming hairy-leaved perennial with small white summer flowers, giving little hint of the color locked in its root; because the taproot needs two to three years of growth before it holds enough pigment to be worth harvesting, this is a patience crop rather than a quick dye plant. Dig roots in fall of the second or third year, wash them, and either dry them whole for storage or process fresh — the dye is extracted with alcohol rather than water, since shikonin is only poorly water-soluble, and the resulting dyebath is used on silk and wool with an acidic mordant. It prefers loose, well-drained soil in light shade to full sun and resents root disturbance once established, so direct-seed or transplant into its permanent bed while still small.

planting.note: Direct sow or set divisions after last frost into fertile, well-drained soil; this sprawling vining perennial needs two to three years of root growth before its dye content is worth harvesting.

directions: Indian madder is a scrambling, hook-bristled vining perennial in the same genus as European madder, grown across South Asia for the deep red-to-rust dye extracted from its slender roots and long valued in Ayurvedic medicine under the name manjistha. It climbs over neighboring supports using recurved prickles on its square stems and whorled leaves, so give it a trellis, fence, or shrubby companion to scramble through rather than staking it upright. Roots are dug in fall of the second or third year, washed, and either used fresh or dried and ground for dye extraction; the pigment (chiefly purpurin along with munjistin, distinct in balance from the alizarin-dominant palette of European Rubia tinctorum) gives warmer, more orange-leaning reds on alum-mordanted wool and silk than European madder's cooler brick reds. It tolerates a wider range of climates than its Mediterranean relative, growing successfully through warm-temperate and subtropical gardens where full-sun, alkaline-soil European madder can struggle in summer heat.
